newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan Formosa denies China power plant report.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan Formosa denies China power plant report.

text.p: Taiwan giant Formosa Group on Tuesday denied local media reports it had begun building a US$3 billion thermal power plant in China's coastal Fujian province.
"Formosa has no knowledge of the power plant construction and will take no part in it," group spokesman Su Chi-yi told Reuters by telephone.
Taiwan's Economic Daily News said on Tuesday that Formosa has started construction on a thermal power plant in Fujian with capital provided by the group's U.S. subsidiary.
Su declined to comment on the U.S. unit's plans and said Formosa would obey Taiwan government regulations.

In June, group leaders Formosa Plastics, Nan Ya Plastics Corp and Formosa Chemical and Fiber announced plans to build the $3 billion, 3,600-megawatt Fujian plant in partnership with Fujian authorities.

The group applied for Taiwan state approval but publicly backed out two months later after Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui appealed to local enterprises to slow their investments in the arch rival Chinese mainland.

Lee has argued that Taiwan needed to review its policy of targeting China as a main market for fear that over-dependence on China investment could increase Taiwan's political vulnerability in their half century-old rivalry.

Taiwan has not stopped approving mainland investments but Formosa's decision to suspend the Fujian deal and a similar move by giant President Enterprises on its own China power station plan suggest that Lee's moral appeal has worked.
Taiwan investments in China must be routed indirectly through Hong Kong or other third places and must have Taiwan government approval.
Taiwan officials concede, however, that there is little they can do if local firms choose to route investments through overseas subsidiaries.

Taiwan and China have been rivals since a civil war split them in 1949, with Beijing's communist government seeing the Nationalist-ruled island as a renegade province that ultimately must be reunified with the mainland.

Nearly 30,000 Taiwan firms have poured more than US$20 billion into mainland China since a political thaw in the late 1980s, but the flow slowed in 1996 in the face of political tensions and Lee's go-slow appeals.
